name: Vermilion body paint (Colombia)

lead: Indigenous peoples across the Americas have long painted the face, body and hair with a red pigment made from the seeds of the annatto tree (Bixa orellana), known as achiote, bija or urucum. The paint colours the skin red-orange and is used for decoration, ritual and identity.
The tree is nicknamed the lipstick tree for this cosmetic use. Its colour comes from the carotenoids bixin and norbixin.

paras: Seeds are crushed or processed into a paste and applied to skin, face or hair as paint. Practice, meaning and patterns differ between peoples; this entry does not describe any single Colombian community's methods.

Annatto is regarded as safe for most people at typical food amounts, but it can rarely cause allergic reactions including hives and possibly anaphylaxis, according to a 2025 review cited on Wikipedia.

angle.text: The pigment directly colours skin and hair red-orange. People use it for ceremonial and decorative looks, and the plant's lipstick-tree nickname reflects the cosmetic use.

lead: Red body paint made from annatto seeds (achiote, bija, urucum) has been used by Indigenous peoples of the Americas to decorate the body, face and hair, and to mark the body as protection against evil spirits and illness [1][2]. It is applied to change appearance directly, adding a bold red colour to skin.

Annatto was probably first used for ritual and decorative body painting, sunscreen, insect repellent and medicine rather than as a food additive [1]. Groups named in coverage include Amazonian peoples, the Taíno, and the Tsachila of Ecuador, whose men dye their hair orange with crushed seeds [1][2].
This entry concerns the pigment tradition in the Americas, including Colombia. No source reviewed documents a specific Colombian community's practice in detail, so descriptions are general.

paras: The orange-red colour comes mainly from bixin, which is fat-soluble, and norbixin, its water-soluble form. Unlike beta-carotene, annatto pigments are not vitamin A precursors [1].
The name achiote comes from Nahuatl, and urucu or urucum comes from Tupi, where it means red colour and also refers to the body paint made from the seeds [2].

Indigenous peoples across North, Central and South America used the seeds for red body and face colouring [2]. Body painting remains important among some Brazilian Indigenous groups such as the Wari' [1].
No studies found. A 2025 review found annatto safe for most people in typical food amounts, with rare allergic reactions [1].
